newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's Cimpor increases profits by 7.3 percent.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's Cimpor increases profits by 7.3 percent.

text.p: Portugal's biggest cement group Cimpor-Cimentos de Portugal on Wednesday posted a 7.3 percent hike in 1996 profit to 19.7 billion escudos ($116 million), which it attributed to favourable market conditions and improved efficiency.

A statement said the profit increase was due to "the good behaviour of most markets in which Cimpor operates, particularly Portugal, improved industrial efficiency and the inclusion in the second half of results from its activities in Morocco."
Last August Cimpor bought Moroccan cement firm Asment Temara for 11.8 billion escudos ($69 million).

Cimpor expected to boost turnover by 15 to 20 percent in 1997, compared with 1996, its president Antonio Sousa Gomes said. "Turnover should grow (in 1997) by at least 15 percent and probably up to 20 percent," he told a news conference.
"Turnover is expected to reach 250 billion escudos by 2000, and productive capacity between 13 and 15 million tonnes."
Cimpor reported that turnover stood at 128.3 billion escudos in 1996, up from 118.7 billion in 1995.
The company announced an increase in its proposed 1996 dividend to 125 escudos per share from 115 in 1995.
It said it made an extraordinary net profit of 7.7 billion escudos from the sale of its stake in privatised bank Banco de Fomento e Exterior.
Cimpor said its recent acquisitions in Brazil and Morocco had made it possible to raise its productive capacity by 53 percent to 11 million tonnes.
The company planned to borrow up to $300 million, via commercial paper and medium- and long-term bonds, to help pay for the acquisitions in Brazil, Sousa Gomes said.
In its first foray into Brazil, Cimpor acquired cement producer CISAFRA and the SERRANA group's cement business for 62 billion escudos in January this year.
Cimpor's acquisitions in Brazil were expected to account for more than 10 percent of the group's turnover and eight percent of its operating profit in 1997, Sousa Gomes said.
He added that Cimpor had no plans for further company purchases in the short-term, preferring to concentrate on integrating recent acquisitions.
"Unless the conditions were exceptionally attractive, no further purchases are expected," he said.
